title: Texas Foreclosure CTL Requirements — State-Specific Policy
content:
Texas Foreclosure Clear-To-List Policy — State-Specific Requirements.

Overview: Texas is a non-judicial foreclosure state. Foreclosure sales are conducted as public auctions on the first Tuesday of each month at the county courthouse. Texas foreclosure procedures are governed primarily by Texas Property Code Chapter 51.

Section 1 — Foreclosure Sale Verification:
Before a Texas foreclosure property can be listed for resale, verify that the foreclosure sale was conducted in compliance with Texas Property Code Section 51.002. This requires: (a) written notice of default was sent to the borrower at least 20 days before notice of sale, (b) notice of sale was filed with the county clerk and posted at the courthouse door at least 21 days before the sale date, (c) the sale was conducted between 10:00 AM and 4:00 PM on the first Tuesday of the month at the designated county sale location, and (d) the trustee's deed has been properly recorded.

Section 2 — No Statutory Right of Redemption:
Texas does not provide a statutory right of redemption for non-judicial foreclosure sales of non-homestead properties. Once the foreclosure sale is completed and the trustee's deed is recorded, title transfers immediately. This simplifies the CTL process compared to judicial foreclosure states with redemption periods. Exception: Texas Tax Code Section 34.21 provides a two-year redemption period for properties sold for delinquent taxes. Verify no tax sale redemption period is outstanding.

Section 3 — HOA Lien Priority in Texas:
Texas Property Code Chapter 209 governs property owners' association (POA/HOA) assessment liens. In Texas, an HOA's assessment lien is generally subordinate to a first-lien mortgage. However, the HOA may have priority for assessments that came due during the period from the date the first lien was created. After foreclosure of the first lien, the purchasing servicer should verify whether the HOA has filed a separate lien for post-foreclosure assessments. Delinquent HOA assessments must be resolved as part of CTL per baseline policy thresholds.

Section 4 — Tax Lien Priority:
Property tax liens filed by the county tax assessor-collector take priority over all other liens in Texas, including first-lien mortgages. Before listing, verify that all ad valorem property taxes are current. Delinquent property taxes are an absolute CTL blocker — the property cannot be listed until taxes are paid or a payment arrangement is documented. County tax certificates should be obtained to confirm current status.

Section 5 — Valuation Thresholds for Texas:
BPO staleness threshold for Texas foreclosure properties is 60 days, stricter than the 90-day baseline. Texas markets, particularly in Dallas-Fort Worth, Houston, Austin, and San Antonio metropolitan areas, can experience rapid price movement. A 60-day maximum ensures listing prices reflect current market conditions. AVM variance threshold remains at the 15 percent baseline.

Section 6 — Occupancy and Property Preservation:
If the property is confirmed vacant, it must be secured and properly maintained. Texas requires posting of a notice identifying the new owner (or servicer) at the property. For occupied properties, Texas Property Code Chapter 24 governs forcible entry and detainer proceedings. Self-help eviction is not permitted. If the former borrower or tenant remains in possession, an FED action must be filed in Justice of the Peace court. Typical timeline from FED filing to writ of possession is 21 to 40 days depending on county.

Section 7 — Texas-Specific Disclosures:
Texas Property Code Section 5.008(e) provides an exemption from the standard seller's disclosure for foreclosure properties. However, any known material defects including foundation issues, flooding history, or environmental contamination must still be disclosed under common law fraud prevention principles. Properties located in a designated flood zone require disclosure regardless of exemption.

Section 8 — Dallas County Special Requirements:
For properties located in Dallas County, verify that no pending eminent domain proceedings have been filed by the City of Dallas, Dallas County, or TXDOT. Dallas County has an active urban development program that may affect property availability. Check Dallas County Clerk records for any condemnation filings.

References: Texas Property Code Chapter 51 (Power of Sale), Texas Property Code Chapter 209 (Property Owners' Associations), Texas Property Code Chapter 24 (Forcible Entry and Detainer), Texas Tax Code Section 34.21 (Redemption of Property Sold for Taxes).
